YouTube Crypto Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Investment Channels

Fake YouTube crypto channels are designed to look identical to the real thing — but one wrong click can cost you thousands.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-06 · 9 min read

Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What YouTube crypto scams look like

YouTube crypto scams typically involve fake channels or accounts impersonating real crypto experts, YouTubers, or financial personalities. The scammer creates a channel with a nearly identical name — often differing by just one letter or character — and uploads videos or hosts live streams promoting a fake cryptocurrency investment platform. They may claim to be running a limited-time giveaway, offering to double your Bitcoin, or promoting an exclusive investment opportunity with guaranteed returns. The fake channel often includes stolen footage from the real creator, professional-looking graphics, and comments from fake accounts praising the investment.

Viewers are directed to click a link in the video description or comments, which takes them to a fraudulent website designed to mimic a legitimate crypto exchange or investment platform. Once there, they are asked to deposit money or cryptocurrency, which disappears immediately. The scammer may also use YouTube comments on popular crypto videos to post links to their fake channel or investment site, targeting viewers already interested in cryptocurrency.

Red flags that reveal a YouTube crypto scam

  • The channel name is almost identical to a famous creator's but with a slight variation — check the exact spelling and look for a blue verification tick next to the real creator's name.
  • The video promises guaranteed returns, quick profits, or 'doubling your money' — legitimate investments never guarantee returns.
  • You are asked to deposit money or send cryptocurrency to an external website or wallet address linked in the video description.
  • The live stream chat is full of fake accounts with generic names praising the investment and sharing their 'profits' — real viewers rarely all agree unanimously.
  • The video uses urgency language like 'limited time only', 'act now', or 'spots filling up fast' to pressure you into deciding quickly.
  • The creator's upload history is very recent or sparse, or the channel suddenly started posting crypto content after years of different topics.
  • The website you are directed to has a slightly different URL from the real platform — for example, using a hyphen or different domain extension.
  • The 'investment platform' asks you to verify your identity by uploading a photo of your passport or driving licence before you can withdraw funds.

How the scam unfolds from first click to money loss

The scam typically begins when you watch a YouTube video — either on a fake channel or in a comment on a legitimate video — promoting a crypto investment opportunity. The video or comment includes a link to what appears to be a professional investment platform. When you click the link, you arrive at a website that looks almost identical to a real crypto exchange, complete with login pages, account dashboards, and charts showing rising prices. You are prompted to create an account and verify your email.

The site then asks you to deposit money via bank transfer, debit card, or cryptocurrency. Once you send the money, it is transferred to the scammer's account, and the fake website either stops responding or shows fake 'profits' in your account that you cannot actually withdraw. If you try to withdraw, you may be told you need to pay a 'tax' or 'verification fee' to release your funds — another layer of the scam. By this point, your money is gone, and the fake channel or website disappears or goes offline.

Some scammers may also use the personal information you provided during account creation for identity theft or to target you with follow-up scams.

How to verify if a YouTube crypto channel is genuine

Before clicking any link or depositing money, take these verification steps. First, check the channel name letter-by-letter against the creator's official website or social media accounts — scammers often use lookalike names with subtle differences. Look for a blue verification tick next to the channel name; YouTube awards these to established, authentic creators, though they are not foolproof. Visit the creator's official website or verified social media accounts (Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn) and check if they have ever mentioned the investment platform or giveaway you saw.

If the creator is a real public figure, search their name plus 'YouTube scam' to see if they have publicly warned about impersonators. Never click a link from a YouTube comment or video description without first checking the channel's history — legitimate creators have consistent upload patterns and established audiences. If the video is a live stream, check the channel's creation date and subscriber count; new channels with few subscribers promoting investment schemes are almost always scams.

Finally, independently verify the investment platform by searching for its name plus 'scam' or 'reviews' — if it is fraudulent, you will likely find warnings from other victims.

What to do immediately if you have already sent money

If you have deposited money or cryptocurrency to a fake investment platform, act quickly. First, stop all contact with the scammer and do not send any additional money, even if they claim you need to pay a fee to unlock your funds. If you used a debit or credit card, contact your bank immediately and report the transaction as fraudulent; your bank may be able to reverse the payment or dispute the charge.

If you sent cryptocurrency, report the wallet address to the blockchain platform and your crypto exchange — they cannot recover the funds, but the information helps track scammers. Change the password on your YouTube account and any other accounts that share the same email or password. If you provided personal information such as your passport number, driving licence, or date of birth, monitor your credit file through Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion for signs of identity theft, and consider registering for Cifas Protective Registration at cifas.org.uk to add a fraud alert to your name.

Do not attempt to contact the scammer or the fake website again, as this may expose you to further manipulation or additional scams.

How to report YouTube crypto scams in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to maximise the chance of action. Report the fake YouTube channel directly to YouTube by clicking the three-dot menu on the channel or video and selecting 'Report channel' or 'Report video' — describe it as impersonation or fraud. Report the fraudulent website to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) by forwarding the details to report@phishing.gov.uk. If you lost money, report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040, https://www.reportfraud.police.uk) if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 (https://www.scotland.police.uk/contact-us/non-emergencies/) if you are in Scotland.

For consumer advice and support, contact Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 if you are in England or Wales, Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 800 9060 if you are in Scotland, or Consumerline on 0300 123 6262 if you are in Northern Ireland. If the scam involved a cryptocurrency transaction, also report it to your crypto exchange or wallet provider, as they may be able to flag the receiving wallet address.

Protecting yourself from YouTube crypto scams going forward

Be sceptical of any YouTube video or comment promoting investment opportunities, especially those promising quick or guaranteed returns. Never click links from video descriptions or comments without verifying the channel's authenticity first — use the verification steps above every time. Assume that any unsolicited investment opportunity on YouTube is a scam unless you have independently confirmed it through the creator's official website or verified social media. Enable two-factor authentication on your YouTube account and any cryptocurrency exchange accounts you use, making it harder for scammers to access your accounts if they obtain your password.

Be wary of live streams, as scammers often use them to create a false sense of urgency and community — the chat may be filled with fake accounts praising fake profits. If a creator you follow suddenly starts promoting crypto investments, check their official channels first; their account may have been hacked. Educate yourself about how legitimate cryptocurrency exchanges work and what their security features look like, so you can spot obvious fakes. Finally, remember that if something sounds too good to be true — especially a promise of quick, easy, or guaranteed returns — it almost certainly is.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell if a YouTube channel is really run by the crypto expert I think it is?

Check for a blue verification tick next to the channel name — this is YouTube's official mark of authenticity. Compare the channel name letter-by-letter with the creator's official website or verified social media accounts; scammers often use names that differ by just one character. Visit the creator's official website or Twitter account and see if they have ever mentioned the investment platform or giveaway you saw — legitimate creators will warn their audience about impersonators.

I clicked a link from a YouTube video and deposited £500 to a crypto investment site. Can I get my money back?

Contact your bank immediately and report the transaction as fraudulent; they may be able to reverse the payment if it was made by debit or credit card. If you sent cryptocurrency, the funds are almost certainly unrecoverable, but report the wallet address to your crypto exchange and the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, so it is recorded and investigated.

What should I do if I see a YouTube comment promoting a crypto investment with a link?

Do not click the link. Instead, report the comment to YouTube by clicking the three-dot menu next to it and selecting 'Report comment' — describe it as spam or scam. If the comment is on a video by a real creator, let them know by replying to the comment or contacting them through their official channels, as they may not be aware of the impersonation.

Is it safe to use a cryptocurrency exchange that is advertised on YouTube?

No legitimate, established cryptocurrency exchange needs to advertise on YouTube to attract users. If you see an exchange being promoted in a video or comment, assume it is a scam unless you have independently verified it through multiple sources — check reviews on independent crypto forums, search for the exchange name plus 'scam', and confirm its website URL matches what you find on official sources, not the link in the video.

I provided my passport number and email to a fake investment site. What should I do?

Change the password on your email account immediately and enable two-factor authentication. Monitor your credit file through Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion for signs of identity theft. Register for Cifas Protective Registration at cifas.org.uk to add a fraud alert to your name, which makes it harder for scammers to open accounts in your name. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
